Processes of 
Labor and Birth
NRBS 3410
Summer 2026

2
Labor & Birth Assessment Data
 Name, age, ethnicity
 Obstetric care provider
 Presenting complaint
 Last menstrual period (LMP)
 Due Date (EDD)
 GPTAL
 Current medications (Rx, OTC, 
herbal, homeopathic)
 Allergy history
 Current and pre-pregnant weights
 Prenatal care (number of visits)
 Prenatal lab results and treatments
 Amniotic membrane status
 Onset and frequency of contractions
 Description of vaginal bleeding
 Location and description of 
discomforts
 Time last fetal movement felt
 Ultrasound, NST, or other prenatal 
testing and results
 Medications and treatments
 Complications such as UTI, bleeding, 
infection, malpresentation, 
hypertension, GDM

3
Obstetrical History
 Number, spacing, and outcomes of pregnancies
 Birth methods, including surgical incision type
 Pregnancy-related disorders
 Preeclampsia
 Preterm labor
 Gestational diabetes
 Birth complications
 Instrumental birth
 Hemorrhage
 Abnormal placenta
 Postpartum depression

4
Psychosocial Data
 Family status
 Adequate labor support
 Employment status
 Adequacy of living conditions
 Financial needs
 Able to provide car seat, infant care items, and food

5
Childbirth & Parenting Preferences
 Prenatal education type
 Written birth plan?
 Labor and postpartum support strategy
 Plan for managing labor pain
 Preferences regarding medical interventions
 Pediatric care provider
 Infant feeding method
 Rooming in?
 Circumcision?

The Theories of the Onset of Labor
 Uterine stretch-The uterine myometrium is 
stretched by fetus
 Progesterone withdrawal- estrogen to 
progesterone ratio changes
 Increased oxytocin sensitivity-receptors 
increase at end of pregnancy
 Increased release of prostaglandins-
increased oxytocin levels stimulate 
prostaglandin release.

Premonitory Signs of Labor
Premonitory-”give warning to”
Cervical changes (cervical softening, possible cervical dilation)
 Cervical collagen undergo enzymatic changes fibers absorb water, 
soften and lengthen  
Lightening-movement of fetal presenting part into maternal pelvis- 
breathing eases, urination may increase
 Engagement- fetal presenting part reaches zero station
Increased energy level (nesting)- epinephrine release 24-48 hours before 
labor
Bloody show-Loss of mucous plug
Braxton Hicks contractions 30 seconds average. Pulling up/tightening of top 
uterus
Spontaneous rupture of membranes-sudden gush or continuous leak.
 Risk of prolapsed cord without engagement

False vs. True Labor
FALSE
Irregular contractions
 Felt in abdomen
 Do not Increase
Stops with change in position: 
walking or resting stops or 
lessens contractions
No cervical change: no dilation
No “descent”of fetus through 
the birth canal
TRUE
 Contractions increase in 
regularity and intensity
 Stronger and closer 
together
 Contractions may begin in 
lower back, radiates to front 
 No difference with position 
changes.  Contractions 
continue regardless
 Cervical changes: cervical 
dilatation and/or efffacement
 Descent of fetus through birth 
canal
8

Questions to Ask
 Contraction timing-
 How frequent are contractions”
 How long do they last?
 Contraction strength
 Do they increase over time?
 Contraction discomfort
 Do contractions interfere with normal activities. 
Can you work, talk, function through them?
 Change in contraction activity-
 What happens if you rest or walk?
 Any leakage of fluid? (ROM)

Stay or Go?
False Labor
Rule out True Labor
 Have a snack and drink 
fluids
 Walk around 
If contractions diminish in 
intensity or pattern. Stay home
True Labor
When to come to hospital 
 Contractions are 5 minutes 
apart
 Last 45-60 seconds
 Conversation is not possible
 Membranes have ruptured

Natural Labor 
 Cervical effacement and dilation occur without medication or 
intervention
 Labor Induction
 If cervix is not soft or “ripe” and not effaced
 Stimulation to initiate cervical effacement 
 dilation may follow without additional intervention
 Cervical Ripening with a vaginal prostaglandin
 Cervadil given in 2 doses 12 hours apart
 Cytotec given every 4 hours x 4 doses
Oxytocin used to induce labor or enhance ineffective contractions
 Make contractions longer and stronger - risk is hyperstimulation!! Need to 
assess, and stop infusion if contractions > 90 seconds
 Side effects:abruptio placenta, rupture
 Oxytocin is given routinely postpartum to contract uterus

Oxytocin Dosing
 Concentration is 10 milliunits/mL in 1L bag
    = 10,000 milliunits/L
 0.5 to 2 milliunits/minute IV loading dose
 Increases of 1 to 2 milliunits every 15 to 40 minutes 
until there is an established contraction pattern

Contraindication for Labor Induction
 Previous cesarean section
 Placenta previa
 Vasa Previa
 Umbilical vessels are not at center of placenta
 May be at side (velamentous insertion)
 Placenta may be bi-lobed with vessels entering at 
different spots

Factors Affecting Labor and Birth 
(“5 P’s”)
 Passageway (birth canal: bony pelvis & soft tissues)
 Passenger (fetus and placenta)
 Powers (contractions) 
 Position (maternal) 
 Psychological response

Passageway: Bony Pelvis
 Linea terminalis: division of false and true pelvis 
 True pelvis (below linea terminalis)
 Inlet-wider in transverse measurement
 Mid-pelvis
 Outlet- bounded by ischial tuberosities (pelvic 
measurements)
 False pelvis (above linea terminalis)
 Upper flared parts of 2 iliac bones and concavities
 Wings of base of sacrum

Linea Terminalis
Plane of Pelvic Inlet (True Pelvis)

Passageway: Bony Pelvis(cont’d.)
 Pelvic shape
 Gynecoid: favorable for vaginal delivery
 About 50% of women have true gynecoid pelvis
 Inlet is round, outlet is expansive
 Diameters at all angles can accommodate fetal head
 Android: male-shaped, not favorable 
 Heart shaped, funneled 
 20% of women have android pelvis
 Descent is slow
 High rate of cesarean
 Anthropoid: usually adequate
 25% of women
 Inlet is oval sacrum is long=deep pelvis
 Wider front to back 
 Platypelloid: not favorable
 Least common 5%

Passageway: Soft Tissues
 Cervix
 Effacement-thinning of cervix
 Thins through enzymatic changes that allow for cellular realignment.
 Effacement to allow presenting part to descend into vagina
◦ Effaces:  thins and shortens 2.5-3cm before labor
 0-100%
 Occurs during the first stage of labor for most multiparas 
 May occur before dilation in primipara (can efface during last weeks of 
pregnancy) 
◦ Dilates:  opens widening the outlet
 0 cm to 10 cms
 Full dilitation marks the end of the first stage of labor
 May occur simultaneously with effacement first in multipara
 Response to uterine contractions and hormone influence 
(prostaglandins)
 Vagina- rugated tissue expands and stretches to accommodate the 
fetus

Fig. 15-11. Cervical effacement and dilation. Note how cervix is drawn up around presenting 
part (internal os). Membranes are intact, and head is not well applied to cervix. A, Before labor. 
B, Early effacement. C, Complete effacement (100%). Head is well applied to cervix. D, 
Complete dilation (10 cm). Cranial bones overlap somewhat, and membranes are still intact.

Passenger
Fetal head is largest part of fetus- 25% of body surface 
IDEAL=smallest fetal skull diameter to pass through largest 
maternal pelvic diameter-see next slide 
(suboccipitobregmatic)
Fetal skull-2-frontal, 2-parietal, 1-occipital not yet fused
 Allows overlapping sutures (connective tissue) decreases 
dimensions 0.5 to 1 cm. 
 Sutures help identify fetal position- via anterior and posterior 
fontanelles
 Molding is the elongation of the fetal head by the overlapping 
of cranial bones during birth.  Resolves on it’s own
 Caput Succedaneum-edema of fetal scalp tissues from 
pressure
 Cephalohematoma-hematoma beneath fetal skull
 Diameters that effect the birth process most: 
suboccipitobregmatic 9.5 cm, and biparietal 9.25 cm
 Suboccipitobregmatic is the smallest diameter of skull
Fetal Skull

Nursing Role During Labor
 Fetal assessment-assess fetal well-being
 Determined by Fetal Heart Rate Assessment
 Labor progress-Pattern and progression of contractions
 Maternal and fetal tolerance of labor
 Maternal -Vital Signs, Pain Assessment, Psychological Assessment
 Fetal Heart Rate Patterns
 Pain management
 I & O- NPO? IV Fluid Hydration
 Vital signs-Frequency changes with labor progression
 Exchange of information with CNM/MD
24

25
Vaginal Exam

26
Preparation for a Vaginal Exam
 Explain the procedure
 Assess for latex allergies
 Provide for privacy as able
 Assemble supplies
 Position with thighs flexed and abducted
 Drape with flap to access perineum
 Inform client before touching

27
Supplies for a Digital Vaginal Exam
 Gloves (sterile if membranes ruptured)
 Water-based lubricant
 Nitrazine paper
 Sterile Q-tip
 Slide

28
Vaginal Exam Findings
 Cervical dilatation
 Cervical effacement
 Fetal position
 Fetal station
 Maternal pelvic adequacy
 Amniotic membrane status
 Amniotic fluid characteristics

The Fetus During Labor
 Fetal attitude-flexion or extension of fetal joints 
 Chin against chest/back rounded/knees/elbows/hips flexed 
tightly
 Fetal lie-relationship of fetal and maternal spines
 Longitudinal=lined up together in parallel
 Transverse=fetal spine is perpendicular to maternal
 Fetal presentation-what part of fetus enters the pelvic inlet 
first.
 Cephalic=head first
 Fetal position
 Fetal station
 Fetal engagement

30
Leopold’s Maneuvers
 First maneuver: Identify the fundal contents
 Second maneuver: Locate the fetal back
 Third maneuver: Identify what lies just above the pelvic 
outlet
 Fourth maneuver: Identify the cephalic prominence or brow

Leopold’s maneuvers for determining fetal position, presentation, 
and lie. Note: Some practitioners may perform the sequence 
differently. Many nurses do the fourth maneuver first to identify the 
part of the fetus in the pelvic inlet.

Location of the fetal heart rate (FHR) in relation to the more 
commonly seen fetal positions. The FHR is heard more clearly over

Passenger: Fetal Lie

Cephalic Fetal Presentation
A) Vertex- head well flexed
B) B) Military- head is straight neck not flexed. 
C) C) Brow- neck slightly extended
D) D) Face-neck fully extended

Breech Fetal Presentation
Breech
A) Frank-50-70% buttocks presents, legs extended
B) Full or complete-crossed legged above cervix 5-10%
C) Footling or incomplete- single or D) double footling
 Shoulder

Passenger: Fetal Attitude
Normal is “Fetal Position”

Fetal Position= Where is the fetus in 
relationship to the maternal pelvis?
 Fetal Landmarks to be indentified
 Occipital bone (0): vertex presentation
 Chin (mentum [M]): face presentation
 Buttocks (sacrum [S]): breech presentation
 Scapula (acromion process [A]): shoulder presentation
 Three-letter abbreviation for identification
 1st letter= Right or left side of MOTHER
 2nd letter = what is the presenting part?
 Occiput=O, Mentum=M, Buttocks=S
 3rd letter = MATERNAL aspect of pelvis
 Anterior/Posterior/Transverse

Fetal Engagement
 Presenting part reaching 0 station
 Floating: no engagement; presenting 
part freely movable about pelvic inlet
 Ballottment: fetal presenting part can be 
moved with external manipulation.

Fetal Station: Where is the fetus in 
relation to the MATERNAL ischial spines?
-4 to + 4

Cardinal Movements of Labor
How the fetus travels
 Engagement-fetus reaches the ischial 
spines 0 station. Fetus generally 
enters with sagittal suture in 
transverse
 Descent-downward movement of fetal 
head into pelvic inlet
 Flexion- vertex meets resistance 
(neck flexes)
 Internal Rotation- when occiput 
meets resistance it turns 45° anteriorly 
under pubic symphysis- A/P diameter 
of head= A/P diameter of pelvic outlet
 Extension- occiput under symphysis:  
head extends under pubic arch 
 External Rotation-now free head 
untwists shoulders align for delivery
 Expulsion-birth of the body

Fig. 15-13. Cardinal movements of the mechanism of labor. Left occipitoanterior position. A, 
Engagement and descent. B, Flexion. C, Internal rotation to occipitoanterior position. D, 
Extension. E, External rotation beginning (restitution). F, External rotation.

Powers
 Uterine contractions (involuntary: thin and dilate 
cervix) They are primary stimulus.
 Rhythmic and intermittent. 
 Periods of contraction (decreased blood flow to 
placenta)
 Periods of relaxation between 
 Goal of uterine contractions is to thin and dilate the 
cervix.
 Push presenting part toward lower uterine segment
 Intra-abdominal pressure from mother pushing and 
bearing down in 2nd stage 
 Affected by maternal ability
 Anxiety, fatigue, medications

Uterine Contractions
 Contractions: Three parameters
 Frequency- how often contractions are occurring
 Measured from beginning of one to beginning of another
 Duration-how long contraction lasts- from 
beginning of contraction to end of contraction
 Intensity-determined by manual palpation, or 
internal measurement with a intrauterine 
pressure catheter. (IUCP)

Electronic Fetal Monitoring
Non-invasive
External Fetal Monitoring-records fetal and uterine activity tracing
  1)  Toco-transducer-pressure sensitive-placed on fundus
 Detects changes in uterine pressure
2) Ultrasound transducer-
 Fetal heart rate baseline
 Variability in fetal heart rate
 Accelerations
 Decelerations
INVASIVE: Internal Fetal Monitoring-scalp electrode- small spiral wire placed 
under fetal scalp records fetal heart tracing.  Itrauterine pressure cather 
(IUPC)
 More accurate, no loss of contact with fetal movement
 No maternal artifact
 Membranes must be ruptured to place 
 IUPC can measure true strength of contraction

Psychological Response
 Factors Influencing a Positive Birth Experience 
 Clear information on procedures-what is happening and 
why
 Companion-Studies demonstrate labor support reduces 
maternal complications, cesarean sections, medication 
requirements and improves fetal outcomes and 
maternal emotional well-being (Cochrane 2019)
 Sense of mastery, self-confidence
 Trust in staff caring for her-fear inhibits uterine blood 
flow and placental perfusion
 Positive reaction to the pregnancy
 Personal control over breathing-relaxation helps birth 
processes
 Preparation for the childbirth experience

Physiologic Responses to Labor: Maternal
 Increased heart rate 10-20 bpm.
 Cardiac output- increased 12-31% 1st stage, 50% 2nd stage
 B/P up 35 mmHg (during contractions)
 Increased white blood cell count=25-30,000
 Increased respiratory rate and oxygen consumption-tachypnea 
common
 GI-decreased gastric motility, absorption, gastric pH = increased risk 
for vomiting and aspiration
 Slight temperature elevation
 Muscle aches/cramps
 Increased BMR
 Decreased blood glucose levels-related to glucose utilization and stress 
of labor

Physiologic Responses to Labor: Fetal
 Periodic FHR accelerations and slight 
decelerations 
 Decrease in circulation and perfusion-related to 
uterine contractions- healthy fetus tolerated well
 Increase in arterial carbon dioxide pressure, 
decrease in arterial oxygen pressure (PCO2, PO2)
 Increased risk for acidosis
 Decrease in fetal breathing movements

STAGES of LABOR
 First
◦ onset of labor to full dilation (10 cm)
 Average 3-16+ hours
 Second 
◦ full dilation to birth of infant
 Average 10 minutes to 3 hours
 Third
◦ birth of infant to expulsion of placenta
 Average up to 20 minutes
 Fourth
◦ expulsion of placenta to appx 1-4 hours 
◦ Hemodynamic stability
52

Stages of Labor
 First stage 
 Onset labor to complete cervical dilatation (10 cm)
 Visceral pain-cervical dilation stretching of lower uterine segment
 Longest of all stages
 Three phases of First Stage
 Latent (early) phase- 0-5 cm dilation, effacement 0-40%
 Uterine contractions (UC) every 5-10 minutes 30-45 sec long
 9 hours nullipara vs. 6 hours multipara
 Active phase- begins at 6 cm dilation, 40-80% effacement
 Greatest cervical change
 UC every 3-5 min, 45-60 sec. long
 6 hours nullipara vs. 4 hours multipara
 Average rate of dilation:
◦ 1.2 cm per hour in primigravida
◦ 1.5 cm per hour in multigravida 
 Transition phase- 8-10 cms 80-100% effacement
 UC every 2-3 min, 60-90 sec long
 1 hour nullipara vs 30 min multipara

First Stage of Labor: Continuing Assessment
 Woman’s knowledge, experience, and expectations
 Vital signs- q 15 minutes 
 Vaginal examinations-limit vaginal examinations 
 Changes in maternal attitude or pain level may indicate 
cervical change
 Change in contraction pattern may indicate labor 
progression 
 Uterine contractions
 Pain level
 Coping ability
 FHR
 Amniotic fluid

Maternal Psychological Adaptations
Latent Phase (0-6cm)
 Sense of anticipation, excitement, happiness, relief, 
apprehension
 May express discomfort, grimace with ctx
 Generally alert, talkative and sociable
Active Phase (6-7 cm)
 Anxiety increases
 Fears loss of control
 May exhibit decrease in coping abilty
 Helplessness and increased dependence
 Becomes serious, introverted and concentrated

Transition 8-10 cm
 Cervix becomes part of the lower uterine segment
 Uterine contractions start to put pressure on perineal 
structure 
 Contractions every 2-3 mins; 60-90 secs; strong
 Generally the most difficult time for woman
 Up to 3 hour for primigravida
 15-min to 1 hour for multigravida

Characteristics of Transition
• Amnesia in between cx
• Nausea, vomiting, belching
• leg tremors and involuntary 
shaking
• increased perspiration
• increase in bloody show
• Irritability
• c/o rectal pressure
• Anxiety increases (“can’t take 
it anymore”)
• Restless and/or anger 
• Does not want to be alone
• Inner directed, withdrawn 
and tired
• Generalized discomfort
• Fear of perineal tearing

Nursing care: Transition
 Assessments
 Support and Encouragement
 Breathing Reinforcement
 Minimal handling
 Encourage rest
 Provide information
 Provide privacy

Urge to Push
 Stay with Mom
 Observe non-verbal cues
 May experience urge without completed dilation:  Ferguson’s 
reflex 
 Discourage pushing until full dilation confirmed
 Change breathing to panting or blowing 
 Pushing may be less intense w/multiparous women

Second Stage of Labor
From full dilation 10 cm to delivery of baby
1 hour for nullipara/ less than 30 minutes for multipara
Accomplished by involuntary and voluntary pushing efforts (bearing down) 
with uterine contractions
Open Glottis Pushing-follow mother’s natural urges
NOT holding breath and counting to 10
Delayed Pushing up to 90 minutes
 Demonstrated to reduce pushing time without fetal compromise
 Prevent injury to perineum allow additional stretching
Descent of the presenting part through the pelvis
Station moves from 0 to + 4
May experience urge without completed dilation:  Ferguson’s reflex
Stay with Mom
Change breathing to panting or blowing 
May have mild pushing w/ multipara

Nursing Management: 
Second Stage 
 Assessment
 Typical signs of 2nd stage
 Bearing down
 Report of perineal pressure
 Contraction frequency, duration, intensity
 Maternal vital signs
 Fetal response to labor via FHR
 Continued monitoring with contractions
 Amniotic fluid with rupture of membranes
 Note color and particulate matter or smell
 Green or particulate indication of meconium
 Coping status of woman and partner

Nursing Management: 
Second Stage
 Interventions
 Supporting woman & partner in active decision 
making
 Supporting involuntary bearing-down efforts; 
encouraging no pushing until strong desire or 
until descent and rotation of fetal head well 
advanced
 Providing instructions, assistance, pain relief
 Using maternal positions to enhance descent and 
reduce pain
 Preparing for assisting with delivery

Nursing Management: Second 
Stage (cont’d.)
 Interventions with birth
 Cleansing of perineal area and vulva
Some practitioners wash perineum with betadine
 Assisting with birth, suctioning of newborn, and 
umbilical cord clamping
 Providing immediate care of newborn 
 Drying
 Apgar score
 Identification

Support during Second Stage
 Assist with pushing techniques
 Provide encouragement-mirrors? 
 Reposition frequently-Maternal choice
 Gravity can assist
 Assess bladder, pts with epidural usually have foley I & O
 Prepare for birth- room set-up
 Ongoing fetal assessment-Document FHR every 5 minutes 
during 2nd stage

Third Stage of Labor
Third stage: birth of infant to placental separation
 Placental separation occurs as now empty uterus continues to 
contract
 Signs of separation: 
 Shiny Schultz (smooth shiny fetal side) or Dirty Duncan (beefy 
maternal side) – side that presents is side that separated first. 
 Uterus rises upward
 Umbilical cord lengthens
 Trickle of blood from vagina
 Uterus changes shape-globular
 Placental expulsion-2-30 minutes after delivery
 Fundal massage contracts uterus after placenta is expelled.
 EBL-500 ml for vaginal birth
 1000 ml for cesarean

Fig. 18-25. Third stage of labor. A, Placenta begins the separation process in central portion 
with retroplacental bleeding. Uterus changes from discoid to globular shape. B, Placenta 
completes separation and enters lower uterine segment. Uterus is globular in shape. C, 
Placenta enters vagina, cord is seen to lengthen, and there may be increased bleeding. D, 
Expulsion (birth) of placenta and completion of third stage.

Nursing care during the 3
rd
 Stage 
• Assist w/ perineal repair
• Surgical field/ count
• Assess: 
• Uterine tone- Fundus will be FIRM, well below umbilicus
     approx 4 cms (finger breadths)
• Returns to 1-2 cm (finger breadths) below umbilicus
Approx 4 hours later 
• Vaginal bleeding-amount, color quality
• Vital signs
• Response to anesthesia-epidural most common
return of muscle strength and sensation
• Administration of medications
• Oxytocin/ Pitocin IV or IM
• 20u/1000mL IV fluid or 10u/500mL

4
th
 Stage of Labor
 Recovery Period
 Fourth stage: Up to 4 hours following delivery
 Maternal physiologic adjustment and stabilization
 Focus is on maternal hemo-stabilization and infant bonding
 Immediate hemodynamic stability of mother
 Frequent monitoring- q 15 minute vitals
 Fundal assessment and massage
 Contracted fundus = hemostability
 Bonding
 Skin to Skin contact
 Breastfeeding initiation
